source_document.body:
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine plans to double its drone supplies and more than triple its long-range strike capabilities next year, according to Ukraine’s defense minister, as Kyiv presses ahead with its long-range strike campaign despite the Pentagon’s criticism of attacks deep inside Russia.
Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara made the announcements Tuesday at a press conference after the 37th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group at NATO headquarters in Brussels.
“There are prospects in this, and we are only getting started,” he said.
A day later, the British government said in a statement that it will send Ukraine more than 1,000 long-range strike drones, some able to fly more than 620 miles (1,000 kilometers), in a roughly $342 million (£260 million) package.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to announce the offer Thursday in Berlin at a meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” of Ukraine supporters, where U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steven Witkoff are expected to brief European leaders on peace negotiations.
Ukraine is forging ahead with its long-range strike campaign with support from European partners, despite Washington’s request to prioritize front-line defense and associated midrange strikes instead.
Khmara told the EU Foreign Affairs Council that drones will make up more than half of Ukraine’s weapons needs in 2027. At the press conference, he said 62% of funding should go to drones, including first-person-view, middle-strike, deep-strike and logistics drones.
U.S. negotiators Jared Kushner (center) and Steven Witkoff (right) are welcomed by Günter Sautter (front), the Federal Chancellor’s advisor on foreign and security policy, at the meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing” at the Federal Chancellery in Berlin on Nov. 19, 2026. (Bernd von Jutrczenka/picture alliance via Getty Images)
“While the public conversation focuses on the spectacle of deep strikes designed to incur pain on the Russian population, our assessment is that such strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line,” Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby said in his opening remarks to the meeting.
Such strikes, “especially those that target civilian infrastructure, such as Wildberries, have actually probably hardened the Russian public’s resolve and the Kremlin’s own willingness to escalate,” he said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius responded in a press conference after the meeting, stating that faulting strikes on “strategic military and military use targets” in Russia is “quite a stupid thing, I think.”
“We should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on civil energy, water and heater infrastructure in Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
Colby left the meeting shortly after his own remarks, before the press conference, according to two sources cited by The Telegraph , one of whom said he did not stay for Khmara’s classified briefing.
Colby “definitely appeared more on the side of Russia than on the side of Ukraine,” a German source told the publication.
Colby’s remarks follow pressure from the Trump administration on Kyiv to spare Russian refineries .
Colby also said that strikes that target “Russia’s warmaking machinery can also help contribute to slowing Russia’s advance on the front lines” and that Ukraine should not “be forced to fight with its hands tied behind its back.”
Further support from European allies announced at the meeting included a pledge by Germany to buy jointly produced middle-strike and deep-strike drones, and a promise from Norway to set aside $300 million to buy Ukrainian drones, according to a Defense Ministry readout .
British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said at the same press conference that deep strikes have “helped to degrade Putin’s war machine, buying time and saving lives.” He also said Colby’s attendance in person was “a further demonstration of U.S. commitment and involvement.”
Britain’s new drones will let Ukraine target “military production facilities and other legitimate military targets far behind the front lines,” according to a government statement .
“It’s not for us to tell Ukraine how to fight their war,” Britain’s Streeting said.
